15.title: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
15.hook: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
15.howItsDone: Buddhists practice metta by silently repeating short wishes, such as may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease, first for themselves and then outward to loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings; the Metta Sutta is chanted in monasteries and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anatta, not-self, a question kept open. Your line was look. Week three turns to the heart, starting with a word for friendliness. Day fifteen.

The coworker who replies all. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven on a Saturday. The relative with opinions about your life at every holiday. Not villains. Just people who are hard to like. Maybe a face comes to mind already. Now here's an old Buddhist practice: people sit quietly and wish that person well. On purpose. Not because they've forgiven anything, and not because the person has earned it. Just as training, the way you'd train a muscle. It sounds almost backwards. Buddhists trace it to the Buddha's own teaching.
screen: `THE ONE WHO REPLIES ALL.` → `NOW WISH THEM WELL.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Metta. It's a word in Pali, the old language the Buddha's teachings were kept in. It comes from mitta, a friend. So metta is friendliness. A wish for someone's good, the plain warm kind you'd feel for a friend, pointed at anyone at all. You may know its Sanskrit cousin, maitri, or the name Maitreya, the friendly one, the Buddha that tradition says is still to come. There's a short teaching on it, the Metta Sutta, still chanted in Buddhist homes and monasteries. It pictures a mother protecting her only child with her own life, and says to hold a heart like that toward every living being. Seen and unseen. Near and far. Born and not yet born. Every one. And the Buddha's own verses put the reason bluntly: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule. Not a new idea even then. How do people actually do it? Later teachers laid out a gentle order. Start with yourself, because it's hard to give what you've never felt. Then someone you love. Then someone neutral, the person who sells you coffee. Then, last and slowest, someone difficult. You don't pretend to like them. You just wish them what you'd want: to be safe, to be well, to be at ease. Some who practice it describe an odd side effect: it changes them more than anyone else. The difficult person is still difficult. They just carry less of that person around.
screen: `METTA — FROM MITTA, A FRIEND.` · `LIKE A MOTHER WITH HER ONLY CHILD.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, THE HARD ONE.` · then, large: `MAY YOU BE AT EASE.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Start where the old order starts: with yourself. Breathe in, and on the way out let a few words go: may I be at ease. Then someone you love: may you be at ease. Then a stranger, the person who sells you coffee. Then, if you're ready, that face from a minute ago. You don't have to feel warm. Just let the words go out, one breath at a time.
Metta. Friendliness. A wish for anyone's good, even the people who make it hard. Fifteenth word.
Your line: may you be at ease. You don't have to like someone to wish them well. Day fifteen.

16.title: compassion
16.hook: compassion — metta when it meets pain
16.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate karuna in meditation, extending the wish that beings be free from suffering, and in action: caring for the sick, the poor and animals; in Mahayana traditions people recite the names or mantra of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, friendliness, from the word for a friend. Your line was may you be at ease. Day sixteen.

A friend calls, and you can hear right away that something's wrong. The first instinct might be to fix it. Give advice. Find the silver lining. Change the subject to something lighter. Or the instinct might be to back away a little, because their pain is heavy and there's your own day to get through. Both are normal. Both are ways of leaving. There's a third thing a person can do, and it's much harder than fixing or leaving. You can stay. Today, what metta becomes when it meets pain.
screen: `A FRIEND CALLS, SOMETHING'S WRONG.` → `FIX IT, OR BACK AWAY.` → `OR: STAY.`

segments.voice: Karuna. Compassion. It's the second of four qualities Buddhists call the brahmaviharas, the divine abodes, places a heart can live. Metta, friendliness. Karuna, compassion. Mudita, gladness at others' good fortune. And upekkha, a steady calm, which you'll meet in a few days. Metta wishes someone well. Karuna is what happens when that wish runs into someone's pain. An old commentary, Buddhaghosa's, explains the word this way: compassion is what makes a good heart tremble when others suffer. It doesn't turn away. It quivers, and stays. The same commentary warns about two traps. Compassion's far enemy is cruelty, the plain opposite. Its near enemy is sneakier: a worldly grief that looks like compassion but is really sorrow for oneself. Some modern teachers put the near enemy as pity. Pity looks down: oh, you poor thing, glad that isn't me. Compassion stands beside. There's a story in the monastic rules about this. The Buddha and his attendant Ananda find a monk lying sick in his own filth, and nobody is caring for him. The Buddha washes him himself, with Ananda's help. Then he gathers the monks and says, in effect: you have no mother or father here to care for you. If you don't care for each other, who will? Whoever would care for me should care for the sick. In Mahayana Buddhism, compassion is embodied by Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world, known as Guanyin in China and Chenrezig in Tibet. But it can start very simply. Someone is hurting. You don't look away.
screen: `KARUNA — METTA MEETS PAIN.` · `THE HEART TREMBLES, AND STAYS.` · `PITY LOOKS DOWN. COMPASSION BESIDE.` · `THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.` · then, large: `STAY.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Bring to mind someone who's hurting right now. Someone you know, or someone you saw on the news. Let yourself feel a little of it. Not all of it, just enough that your heart moves. Notice any urge to fix it, or to pull away. Don't act on either. Just stay with them in your mind, breathing. If you like, let a wish go toward them: may you be free from this pain.
Karuna. Compassion: metta when it meets pain, the heart that trembles and stays beside, not above. Sixteenth word.
Your line: stay. Not fixing, not leaving: staying is its own kind of help. See you tomorrow.

17.title: the community
17.hook: the community; why the Buddha said it's the whole of the path
17.tomorrow: the Buddha's past lives as animals
17.howItsDone: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, often by reciting the three refuges in Pali; they support monastic communities with food and gifts, and gather with lay sanghas to meditate, chant, study and celebrate festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karuna, compassion, metta meeting pain. Your line was stay. Day seventeen.

New habits are hard to keep alone. The gym, eating better, an earlier bedtime, meditating every day. A week goes great, and then, quietly, it doesn't. The habits that last often have someone else in them. A running partner. A class. A friend who texts, you coming? Plenty of things are easier with company. The Buddha seems to have thought so too. When his attendant Ananda suggested friends were half the path, the Buddha corrected him.
screen: `A HABIT TRIED ALONE.` → `A HABIT THAT LASTED.` → `SOMEONE ELSE WAS IN IT.`

segments.voice: Sangha. The word means an assembly, a gathering, a community. It's the third of the three jewels you bowed to on day two. The Buddha, the teacher. The Dharma, the teaching. And the Sangha, the community that practices it. In its narrowest sense, the sangha means the monks and nuns. The Buddha is remembered describing a fourfold assembly: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen. Today some Buddhists, especially in Western groups, use sangha for any group that practices together: a temple congregation, a Tuesday-night sitting group, the people you meditate with online. Here's the story from the discourses. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, and his cousin by tradition, says to him one day: it seems to me that good friendship is half of the holy life. And the Buddha answers: don't say that, Ananda. Good friendship, good companionship, is the whole of the holy life. Not half. The whole thing. He explains that a person with good friends can be expected to develop the whole path. The friend doesn't replace the practice. The friend is how the practice keeps going. When an old English translator met the word sangha, he reached for a very English word: the Church. It's a clumsy fit in some ways, but it catches something true. A sangha isn't a club you join because you already agree. It's the people who keep walking beside you on the days you'd rather quit.
screen: `SANGHA — THE COMMUNITY.` · `THE THIRD OF THREE JEWELS.` · `MONKS, NUNS, LAYMEN, LAYWOMEN.` · `NOT HALF. THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `YOU NEED PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Bring to mind the people who walk with you. Not the whole world, just a few faces. The friend who checks in. The teacher who believed in you. Maybe the stranger who sat near you once, in a quiet room. Hold each face for a breath or two. Notice that you didn't get here alone. If you like, let a little metta go to each of them.
The sangha. The community, the third jewel; the people who practice together and keep each other walking. Seventeenth word.
Your line: you need people. Not half the path, the Buddha said: the whole of it. Day seventeen.

18.title: the Buddha's past lives as animals
18.hook: the Buddha's past lives as animals; the monkey king
18.carry: the bridge he made of his body
18.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Jataka stories to children, perform them in dance and drama, paint them on temple walls, and hear them in sermons; in Theravada countries the last ten Jatakas are especially loved, and the Vessantara Jataka is staged at festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sangha, the community, the third jewel. Your line was you need people. Today, a story. Day eighteen.

A huge mango tree grows on the bank of a river. In it lives a troop of monkeys, eighty thousand of them, the story says, and their king. One night a human king's archers surround the tree. They mean to shoot every monkey at dawn. There's no way down. The monkeys are trapped between the arrows and the river. And the monkey king looks across the water at the far bank, and makes a decision. This is one of hundreds of stories Buddhists have told children, and grown-ups, for many centuries. The monkey king, they say, was the Buddha.
screen: `A MANGO TREE BY A RIVER.` → `ARCHERS WAITING FOR DAWN.` → `THE MONKEY KING DECIDES.`

segments.voice: The Jataka. The word means birth stories. They're tales of the Buddha's earlier lives, before he became the Buddha, when he was still on the long way. Buddhist tradition says he lived countless lives, as kings and merchants and poor men, and very often as animals: a hare, a deer, an elephant, a quail, a monkey. The Pali collection has around five hundred and fifty of them, and Jataka scenes are carved in stone on some of the oldest Buddhist monuments in India. Here's the monkey king's story, the way it's told. He leaps across the river to the far bank and ties one end of a long cane to a tree. He ties the other end around his own waist and leaps back. But the cane is too short. He can reach the mango tree only with his hands. So he grips a branch and stretches his body out across the gap. And he tells his monkeys: cross. One by one, all of them run across the cane, and over his back, to safety. His body is torn by it. The human king has watched the whole thing from below. He's so moved that he has the monkey king gently brought down and cared for. And before he dies, the monkey king teaches him what a ruler is for: a king should care for his people the way I cared for mine. Each Jataka ends by telling you who was who, and in this one the monkey king was the future Buddha. Why tell stories like this? Because they show the path from the inside. Generosity. Courage. Compassion. Not as ideas, but as a monkey holding on to a branch until the last one is across.
screen: `JATAKA — BIRTH STORIES.` · `HARE, DEER, ELEPHANT, MONKEY.` · `THE CANE TOO SHORT.` · `A KING LEARNS WHAT RULING IS FOR.` · then, large: `THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Feel your own arms and shoulders, the part of you that would do the holding. Now bring to mind someone trying to get across something right now: a kid with an exam, a friend in a hard month, a coworker drowning in a deadline. Not a grand rescue. Just one small stretch that could help: staying late, holding the door a little longer, listening to the end of the story. Picture holding on while they cross. Notice what it costs, and what it gives.
The Jataka. Birth stories: the Buddha's past lives, many as animals, showing the path from the inside. Eighteenth word.
Your line: the bridge he made of his body. Small stretches count too. That's day eighteen.

19.title: upekkha
19.hook: upekkha; the steady mind in a storm
19.carry: let it be as it is
19.tomorrow: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
19.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate upekkha as one of the four brahmaviharas, often after metta, karuna and mudita, by reflecting that beings meet the results of their own actions, and by practicing steadiness through life's gains and losses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Jataka, the monkey king. Your line was the bridge he made of his body. Day nineteen.
screen: `THE JATAKA — THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Monday, the boss calls the work brilliant, and the whole day floats. Tuesday, a client calls it the worst thing they've seen, and sleep won't come. Wednesday, a friend forgets a birthday. Thursday, a stranger compliments a coat, and suddenly it's fine again. Up, down, up, down, like a boat in weather. Plenty of weeks go like that, and it gets called being human. It is. But the Buddha named those winds, one by one, and taught a way to stand in them without being blown over. Today, the steady mind in a storm.
screen: `MONDAY: BRILLIANT.` → `TUESDAY: THE WORST.` → `A BOAT IN WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Upekkha. Equanimity. It's the fourth of the divine abodes you met with karuna: friendliness, compassion, gladness, and this. The word comes from a root meaning to look, with a prefix meaning over or near. To look on, from a steady place. Not to look away. The Buddha named eight worldly conditions, four pairs, often pictured as winds. Gain and loss. Fame and disgrace. Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. The text says they come to everyone, the untaught and the wise alike. The winds aren't the problem. Getting flung around by them is. The Dhammapada has the picture: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." A rock. The wind still blows. The rock still feels it. It just doesn't move. Here's the part of upekkha that's easy to get wrong. Equanimity isn't indifference. Buddhaghosa warned of its near enemy, a dull, unknowing calm that looks like it but isn't. Some teachers today call that indifference. Indifference says, I don't care. Equanimity says, I care, and I'm not going to be knocked over. It comes last of the four, and here's one way to see why. Metta wishes well. Karuna stays with pain. Mudita is glad for others. And upekkha keeps all of that steady, so the caring doesn't burn you out. A good nurse, a good parent, a good friend in an emergency. Warm, and calm. That's upekkha.
screen: `UPEKKHA — LOOKING ON, STEADY.` · `EIGHT WORLDLY WINDS.` · `THE ROCK IN THE WIND.` · `NOT INDIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit tall and steady, like a rock on a hillside. Now let one wind blow: remember a moment of praise. Notice what it does in your body. Let it pass. Now let the other blow: a moment of blame. Notice that too. Let it pass. Come back to the breath, and to the weight of your body on the seat. The winds come and go. You stay.
Equanimity. Upekkha: looking on from a steady place, a rock in the eight winds. Caring, and not knocked over. Nineteenth word.
Your line: let it be as it is. Letting things be as they are, and still showing up. Day nineteen, done.

20.title: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
20.hook: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
20.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the middle way as the path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, and apply it to everyday practice, balancing effort and ease in meditation, eating, sleep and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: equanimity, upekkha, the rock in the eight winds. Your line was let it be as it is. Day twenty.
screen: `EQUANIMITY — LET IT BE AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: There's a monk named Sona, and he is trying so hard. He's been pacing up and down his walking path in meditation so intensely and for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path is stained with it. And he's getting nowhere. Sitting alone, he starts to think about quitting. Going home. Using his family's money to do some good in the world instead. The Buddha, the sutta says, knows his thought and comes to him. And he doesn't say try harder. He doesn't say give up. He asks about music.
screen: `SONA TRIES SO HARD.` → `HIS FEET ARE BLEEDING.` → `THE BUDDHA ASKS ABOUT MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Before he was a monk, Sona was skilled at the lute, a stringed instrument. So the Buddha asks him: when the strings were too tight, did the lute play well? No. When the strings were too loose, did it play well? No. And when they were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned just right? Then it played beautifully. It's the same with effort, the Buddha says. Too much, and you become restless and strained. Too little, and you become lazy. Find the right tuning. Sona takes the advice, and the story says that before long, he reaches awakening. This is the middle way, and it's where the Buddha's whole teaching began. In the first sermon at the deer park, before he taught the four truths, he told his five companions there are two extremes to avoid. On one side, chasing pleasure: the life he'd had in the palace. On the other, punishing the body: the harsh fasting he'd tried as a seeker. Both, he said, lead nowhere good. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is the eightfold path you already know. So the middle way isn't a bland compromise, halfway between two things. It's more like tuning. A string that's in tune isn't half-tight. It's exactly right for that string, that instrument, that day. And it needs retuning, again and again, because strings drift. Some days need more effort. Some days need rest. The skill isn't finding the answer once. It's listening, and adjusting.
screen: `TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE, TUNED.` · `EFFORT, THE SAME WAY.` · `TWO EXTREMES TO AVOID.` · `NOT HALFWAY. TUNED.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE WAY.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and check your tuning. Is your body too tight? Clenched jaw, raised shoulders, gripping hands? Let a little go. Is it too loose? Slumped, drowsy, drifting? Lift the chest a little and brighten your attention. Look for the place in between: upright and relaxed, awake and easy. When you drift one way or the other, gently retune.
The middle way. Between indulgence and self-punishment, not a compromise but a tuning, adjusted again and again. Twentieth word.
Your line: tune. Not halfway between two things; exactly right for today. That's day twenty.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; "mind is the forerunner"
21.howItsDone: Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, memorize and chant verses of the Dhammapada, hear them explained in sermons with the stories that go with each verse, and keep a copy at home as a small book of daily wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the middle way, the lute string tuned just right. Your line was tune. Day twenty-one.

Three weeks. Look at your strand. Karma, the three jewels, sati, the four noble truths, dana, Vesak, rebirth. Dukkha, tanha, nirvana, the eightfold path. The precepts, anicca, anatta. Metta, karuna, the sangha, the Jataka, equanimity, the middle way. Twenty words, the everyday vocabulary of a Buddhist life. Those are the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing: the Buddha's whole life, told like a serial, from a queen's dream to his last words. So today, from the top of the foothills, a look up at the mountain. One small book of verses, and its very first line.

segments.voice: The Dhammapada. Four hundred and twenty-three short verses, in twenty-six chapters, kept in the Pali canon and remembered as the Buddha's own sayings. Its verses are chanted, memorized and preached on in Buddhist communities to this day. The name has two halves. Dhamma, the teaching, the way things are. And pada, which means a foot, a step, a path, and also a line of verse. So it's the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching, and both are right. Every step is a line. You've already heard it several times in these three weeks: the fragrance that travels against the wind, nirvana as the highest happiness, hatred ceasing by love, the rock in the wind. Now here's where it starts. The very first verse. Modern translators render it something like: mind is the forerunner of all things. An old English translation reads: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Then, across the first two verses, two images. If someone speaks or acts from a harmful mind, pain follows, like the wheel of a cart following the ox's foot. And if someone speaks or acts from a clear, good mind, happiness follows them, "like a shadow that never leaves him." Notice what the first verse is doing. It isn't telling you what to believe about the universe. It's pointing you back at your own mind, the one place you can actually start. The whole path so far, from day one's intention to the noticing and the metta, begins right there.
screen: `423 VERSES, 26 CHAPTERS.` · `DHAMMA + PADA: TEACHING, STEP.` · `MIND IS THE FORERUNNER.` · `THE WHEEL, AND THE SHADOW.` · then, large: `WHAT YOU THINK, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Think back over these three weeks. Let the words drift past: the seed of an intention, three bows, the gatekeeper, the wobble in the wheel, the open hand, the passing leaf, the monkey on the branch. Don't try to remember them all. Just notice which one has stuck. Which came back to you on an ordinary day, without being asked? Hold that one word. Breathe with it. It's yours now.
The Dhammapada. The path of the teaching, verses of the teaching: four hundred and twenty-three verses that start with the mind. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.
